title: Longest Common Subsequence (LCS)
description: Learn how Dynamic Programming solves sequence matching problems by finding the longest ordered subsequence shared between two strings.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) Problem is one of the most important applications of Dynamic Programming for sequence matching.

The objective is to find the longest sequence that appears in the same order in two strings.

Unlike substring matching, characters in a subsequence do not need to remain consecutive, but they must preserve order.

LCS is widely used in text comparison, DNA analysis, plagiarism detection, version control systems, and file synchronization.

sections.title: Why LCS Matters
sections.content:
Modern systems constantly compare sequences.

Examples include comparing source code versions, detecting document similarities, analyzing biological DNA patterns, spell checking, and recommendation systems.

A brute-force approach would try all possible subsequences, but the number of subsequences grows exponentially.

Dynamic Programming solves this efficiently by reusing solutions to smaller comparison problems.
bullets: Appears in bioinformatics and text systems.

sections.title: Understanding Subsequences
sections.content:
A subsequence is formed by removing characters without changing their order.

For example, possible subsequences of ABCDE include ACE, ABD, and BCDE.

However, ECA is not a valid subsequence because the order changes.

LCS focuses on the longest subsequence shared between two strings.

sections.title: Subsequence vs Substring
sections.content:
This is a very important distinction.

A subsequence may skip characters while preserving order.

For example, ACE is a subsequence of ABCDE.

A substring requires consecutive characters.

For example, BCD is a substring of ABCDE, while ACE is not.

sections.title: Why Brute Force Is Inefficient
sections.content:
Suppose a string contains n characters.

The number of possible subsequences becomes 2^n.

Trying every subsequence combination quickly becomes computationally impossible for large strings.

Dynamic Programming avoids this explosion by storing intermediate comparison results.

sections.title: Core Dynamic Programming Idea
sections.content:
LCS uses overlapping subproblems.

When comparing strings recursively, many smaller string comparisons repeat.

Dynamic Programming stores previously computed subsequence lengths inside a matrix.

This eliminates redundant recursive computation.

sections.title: Understanding the LCS Matrix
sections.content:
The heart of the LCS algorithm is the 2D Dynamic Programming table.

Rows represent characters from the first string.

Columns represent characters from the second string.

Each matrix cell stores the length of the longest common subsequence for that specific subproblem.

The matrix gradually fills as comparisons progress.

sections.title: DP Decision Rules
sections.content:
At every matrix cell, the algorithm compares two characters.

Case 1 — Characters Match:
If A[i] equals B[j], the algorithm extends the subsequence length using the diagonal value plus one.

Case 2 — Characters Do Not Match:
The algorithm selects the larger value between the top cell and left cell.

This preserves the best previously discovered subsequence length.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Example
sections.content:
Suppose:
String A = ABCD
String B = ACBD

First, compare A and A. A match is found, so the subsequence length becomes 1.

Next, compare B and C. No match exists, so the algorithm chooses the larger value between the left and top cells.

The matrix continues filling through repeated comparisons.

The final longest common subsequence becomes ABD with length 3.

sections.title: Visualization of Matrix Filling
sections.content:
LCS matrix transitions follow two rules.

Matching characters extend the diagonal value by one.

Mismatched characters choose the larger value between the top and left cells.

This matrix-filling process transforms recursive sequence comparison into structured optimization.

sections.title: LCS Recurrence Relation
sections.content:
The mathematical core of LCS becomes:

if A[i] == B[j]
    dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1
else
    dp[i][j] = max(
        dp[i-1][j],
        dp[i][j-1]
    )

This recurrence drives the entire Dynamic Programming solution.

sections.title: LCS Pseudocode Pattern
sections.content:
The algorithm compares every character in the first string against every character in the second string.

If characters match, the diagonal value increases.

Otherwise, the algorithm selects the larger value between the top and left cells.

This repeated matrix transition is the heart of LCS Dynamic Programming.

sections.title: Python Implementation
sections.content: LCS implementations commonly use a 2D Dynamic Programming matrix to store intermediate subsequence lengths.

sections.title: Complexity Analysis
sections.content:
The LCS algorithm fills every matrix cell once.

If the first string has length n and the second string has length m, the matrix contains n × m subproblems.

This creates O(n × m) time complexity and O(n × m) space complexity.

Dynamic Programming transforms exponential brute-force comparison into scalable polynomial-time optimization.

sections.title: Why LCS Uses Dynamic Programming
sections.content:
LCS contains overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure.

Without Dynamic Programming, recursive comparisons become extremely repetitive.

Dynamic Programming avoids repeated computation by storing intermediate sequence matches.

This dramatically improves scalability.

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
LCS appears in Git version control systems, plagiarism detection, spell checking, DNA sequence matching, file comparison tools, bioinformatics, and text editors.

Many intelligent comparison systems rely heavily on sequence alignment algorithms.

subsections.title: Mistake: Confusing subsequence with substring
subsections.content: Subsequences may skip characters while preserving order. Substrings must remain consecutive.

subsections.title: Mistake: Misunderstanding DP matrix meaning
subsections.content: Each DP cell represents the best subsequence length for smaller string prefixes.

subsections.title: Mistake: Thinking recursion alone is efficient
subsections.content: Pure recursion creates massive repeated comparisons. Dynamic Programming optimization is essential.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
bullets: LCS finds the longest ordered subsequence shared between two strings.
Subsequences preserve order but may skip characters.
Dynamic Programming stores intermediate comparison results.
The LCS matrix represents optimal subsequence lengths.
LCS is widely used in text comparison and bioinformatics.
